title: Preventing Cache Penetration with Bloom Filters
prompt: Your public product/user lookup endpoint (`GET /v1/items/{item_id}`) serves 25,000 QPS normally from Redis 7 (98% hit rate) backed by PostgreSQL 16 (3,000 QPS max capacity). A credential-stuffing/scraping botnet begins sending 18,000 QPS of random non-existent `item_id`s (both invalid formats like `-1`/`abc` and valid-looking UUIDv4s that do not exist in DB). Because these keys are absent in Redis and absent in PostgreSQL, nothing is ever cached in Redis—all 18,000 QPS punch straight through to PostgreSQL, driving DB CPU to 100% and taking down legitimate traffic. Redesign the read path to absorb 50,000+ QPS of non-existent key probes with < 2% DB impact.

spark.summary: Queries for keys that exist in neither Redis nor the database (e.g., negative IDs, scraped random UUIDs, or deleted SKUs) bypass the cache on every single request and hammer the database directly.
spark.keyTakeaway: When traffic spikes expose hidden coupling, block non-existent key floods using a multi-layer shield: strict edge format validation, a fast in-memory/Redis Bloom Filter (or Cuckoo Filter) pre-check, and short-TTL Negative Caching (`__NULL__` sentinels) for keys that pass the filter.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** `GET /v1/items/{item_id}` serves **25,000 QPS** from Redis 7 (98% hit rate) backed by PostgreSQL 16 (**3,000 QPS max**).

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Edge Validation + In-Memory Bloom Filter + Short Negative Cache (Edge Regex/Range -> Bloom Filter (~24 MB) -> Redis Negative Cache -> Postgres (3k QPS)); 6x DB Overload vs. 99% In-Process Bloom Rejection (Botnet (18k QPS) -> Pod Bloom (24 MB) -> Redis (Neg Cache) -> Postgres (3k max)).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Caching `NULL` in Redis for every missed ID without a Bloom filter lets a botnet spray 100M unique random IDs, bloating Redis RAM and evicting legitimate hot keys. Deploy a 3-layer defense within the 128 MB/pod budget: **Layer 1 — Edge Format Validation**: Reject `-1`, `abc`, and out-of-range IDs at the API gateway (`400 Bad Request`) with zero DB/Redis calls.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Bloom filters are a staple across storage and edge security architectures: **Public User/Item Lookup APIs**: Protects OLTP databases from scraping and credential-stuffing floods.

explanation.foundation: Unlike cache stampedes (one hot key), cache penetration attacks non-existent keys:
explanation.core:

learningJourney.title: Enterprise Solution: Edge Format Guard + 24 MB Bloom Filter + Short Negative Cache

explanation.foundation: Deploy a 3-layer defense within the 128 MB/pod budget:
explanation.core:
- **Layer 1 — Edge Format Validation**: Reject `-1`, `abc`, and out-of-range IDs at the API gateway (`400 Bad Request`) with zero DB/Redis calls.
- **Layer 2 — Compact Bloom Filter (~24 MB)**: Size for $n = 20\text{M}$ items at $p = 1\%$ FPR: $m = -\frac{n \ln p}{(\ln 2)^2} \approx 191.7\text{M bits} \approx 23.9\text{ MB}$ with $k = 7$ hash functions. 99% of valid-format missing IDs return `404` in `< 0.1 ms`. Sync new items (+50k/day) via Kafka CDC (or use a Cuckoo/Scalable Bloom Filter if deletes are frequent).
- **Layer 3 — Short-TTL Negative Cache**: For the 1% Bloom false positives (`~180 QPS`, well under 3,000 QPS), cache a `NULL` sentinel in Redis with `EX 60`.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why can a Bloom filter safely return `404 Not Found` immediately when `might_contain(id)` returns `False`?

options.text: Bloom filters have a 0% false-negative rate—if the bit pattern is not set, the item was definitely never inserted
options.feedback: Correct: false positives are possible (1%), so `True` must still check Redis/DB, whereas `False` is 100% authoritative.

options.text: Because Bloom filters store the full JSON payload of every valid item
options.feedback: Bloom filters store only a compact bit array, not payloads.

options.text: Because Redis automatically queries Postgres when a Bloom filter returns `False`
options.feedback: Returning `False` skips both Redis and Postgres.
